## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; numeral before the noun; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-final.
It has no definite article, no indefinite article, a few cases, nominative-accusative alignment, singular and plural, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark future; there is an indirect (reported or inferred) evidential. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs agree with the subject by suffixes; not with the object.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; verb reduplication; a copula; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words left in place; a vigesimal counting base.
Measured morphology: 10 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 0.8 (0 free word … 3 fused), 16 paradigm cells, 2 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns mark number: plural: a prefix (ʘe, from 'all').

| *jeǂ̬e̞selae* |
| --- |
| dog |

‘dog’

| *ʘe-jeǂ̬e̞selae* |
| --- |
| PL-dog |

‘dogs’

**Case.** Nouns take 2 case markers: locative (LOC): a clitic after the noun phrase (ase, from 'head'); dative (DAT): a suffix (ŋaː, from 'give'). The typology leans nom-acc in alignment, but no case marker shows it yet: word order tells subject from object.

| *laːe=jase* |
| --- |
| house=LOC |

‘in the house’

| *jo̞ɤ-ŋaː* |
| --- |
| man-DAT |

‘to/for the man’

**Gender and noun classes.** There is no gender or noun class.

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Future (FUT): a separate word after the verb (kaːʘ̬ʼe, from 'go'). Unmarked: past, perfective, progressive, habitual (left to context).

| *kaːjʘʼaː* | *kaːʘ̬ʼe* |
| --- | --- |
| go | FUT |

‘(it) will go’

**Mood and evidentiality.** Speakers mark how they know: reported (evidential) (REP): a separate word after the verb phrase (taŋa, from 'say').

| *kaːjʘʼaː* | *taŋa* |
| --- | --- |
| go | REP |

‘(it) goes, they say’

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 3SG: a clitic after the verb (saː, from 'he'). Subject pronouns are dropped when the marker is there. No marker yet for 1SG, 2SG, 1PL, 2PL, 3PL (zero).

| *kaːjʘʼaː=saː* |
| --- |
| go=3SG |

‘he/she goes’

**Negation.** Negation is a prefix (te̞, from 'nothing'); the typology calls it preverbal.

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 2 families of 3+ words; 8% of the 701 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **long** *fema* (A, coined 20 kyr ago in the elf proto-language); 3 words have it as their main root, 3 contain it.

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 51 families of 3+ words; 50% of the 701 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **water** *maː* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the elf proto-language); 11 words have it as their main root, 14 contain it.

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

**(1)** ‘The woman sees the dog.’

| *nanaːe* | *jeǂ̬e̞selae* | *ǁəjaɛʘ̬ɘ=saː* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| woman | dog | see=3SG |

/nanaːe jeǂ̬e̞selae ǁəjaɛʘ̬ɘsaː/ · ‹Nanaae yegǂeselae ||eyaegpxesaa.›

<sub>SOV order; the verb carries the subject's 3SG marker</sub>

**(2)** ‘The big dog sleeps in the house.’

| *jeǂ̬e̞selae* | *leǃ̬ʰa* | *laːe=jase* | *ʘə=saː* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dog | big | house=LOC | sleep=3SG |

/jeǂ̬e̞selae leǃ̬ʰa laːejase ʘəsaː/ · ‹Yegǂeselae leg!ha laaeyase pxesaa.›

<sub>LOC is a case clitic; adjective after the noun; the verb carries the subject's 3SG marker</sub>

**(3)** ‘The man will build the boat.’

| *jo̞ɤ* | *aːǀ̬e̞* | *əmɛ=saː* | *kaːʘ̬ʼe* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man | boat | build=3SG | FUT |

/jo̞ɤ aːǀ̬e̞ əmɛsaː kaːʘ̬ʼe/ · ‹Yoơ aag|e emesaa kaagpx'e.›

<sub>FUT is a separate word after the verb; the verb carries the subject's 3SG marker</sub>

**(4)** ‘Do you hear the thunder?’

| *ǂ̬o̞ʔaː* | *d̪ewe̞me̞* | *saɽe* | *sa* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | thunder | hear | Q |

/ǂ̬o̞ʔaː d̪ewe̞me̞ saɽe sa/ · ‹Gǂo'aa deweme saṛe sa?› · rising intonation

<sub>a clause-final question particle, the word for 'if, whether' (as Russian li is both); no question gram is tracked</sub>

**(5)** ‘What does the child bring?’

| *kaenɛ* | *no̞* | *əjʔa=saː* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| child | what | bring=3SG |

/kaenɛ no̞ əjʔasaː/ · ‹Kaene no ey'asaa?›

<sub>the question word stays where the object stands; the verb carries the subject's 3SG marker</sub>

**(6)** ‘I do not drink the milk.’

| *ᵑǀɛ* | *ɛŋemaː* | *te̞-ja* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | milk | NEG-drink |

/ᵑǀɛ ɛŋemaː te̞ja/ · ‹N|e engemaa teya.›

<sub>negation is a prefix</sub>

**(7)** ‘My mother has a boat.’

| *ᵑǀɛ* | *nɛme* | *aːǀ̬e̞* | *taǁ̬ɛ* | *aba* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother | boat | with | COP |

/ᵑǀɛ nɛme aːǀ̬e̞ taǁ̬ɛ aba/ · ‹N|e neme aag|e tag||e aba.›

<sub>possession with 'with' ('my mother (is) with a dog'; Grambank marks neither a 'have' verb nor locational possession, and the lane picked the conjunctional type); 'with' as a postposition (no COM gram)</sub>
